messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 62, Rafael Ortega had spent most of his adult life becoming the kind of psychiatrist other people trusted with unbearable stories. He was a single man who had built a careful life in the United States after leaving Latin America decades earlier, and for years he had kept his own history largely sealed off. In his twenties he had been detained and tortured by state authorities. What stayed with him most sharply were not a tidy sequence of events but fragments that still arrived with brutal force: the sound of men speaking around him in rapid, overlapping voices he could not make out, the presence of uniforms in doorways and corridors, the sickening certainty that the people holding him could do anything they wanted because no one would stop them. Some stretches of that period remained completely blank to him, while other moments were preserved with terrible precision.

In the years after he immigrated, Rafael had tried to make himself into someone defined by competence and usefulness rather than by what had been done to him. He entered medicine, became a psychiatrist, and learned how to move through hospitals and clinics with a calm, measured authority. Yet the setting of his work also carried quiet dangers. A television in a hospital waiting room playing international news, a police officer escorting an agitated patient through the emergency department, or a burst of incomprehensible chatter in a crowded hallway could strike him with no warning. In those moments the memory did not feel like remembering. It arrived as a full sensory reliving, completely real across sight, sound, and bodily feeling, as if time had dropped away and he were back in detention. Because the memory could be triggered instantly by his surroundings, he had come to scan the world for exactly those cues.

As these episodes accumulated, Rafael grew more certain that the old injury had never truly ended. News stories about political violence or state abuses did not simply upset him; they confirmed what he already believed, that institutions meant to protect ordinary people had failed, just as they had failed him. Seeing men in uniform or hearing official language on television brought up not only fear but bitterness that those responsible had never been held to account. He spoke with increasing conviction about having lost his connection to his community and culture. The country he had left no longer felt like his, but neither did the life he had built in America fully repair that rupture. Those meanings sharpened the sting of his triggers: uniforms were not just uniforms, news was not just news, and confused voices were not just background noise. They carried the whole weight of betrayal.

Once the reliving began to return more often, Rafael started organizing his life around not setting it off. He avoided going out unless he had to, especially to places where there might be crowds, police presence, or televisions showing current events. Before nearly any interaction, even routine exchanges, he found himself rehearsing what he would say. He told himself this was simply preparation, but he knew it was also an effort to prevent the disorientation he felt when rapid or unclear speech around him made his body go rigid. When intrusive recollections broke through, he would force his mind onto something else immediately, redirecting himself with professional tasks, mental lists, or deliberately unrelated topics. These habits gave him brief relief, but they also kept the memory poised and unchanged, ready to return in the same total form the next time a cue slipped past him.

Over months and years, the avoidance narrowed his world. Outside of work he spent more time alone in his apartment, limiting invitations and stepping back from social and cultural spaces that once might have anchored him. That retreat deepened his sense that he had lost his community, and the loss in turn made every fresh reminder feel like proof that he had been abandoned by both his country and history. Even at work, where he remained highly skilled, the cycle intruded. If he heard garbled voices through a clinic door, he would tense before entering; if a patient encounter involved security staff, he could feel himself already bracing for the memory. The more he rehearsed and redirected, the more alert he became to danger signals in his surroundings, and the more quickly those signals could pull him back into the sensory force of the torture.

He finally sought help after realizing that the effort required to keep himself composed was beginning to erode the life he had built. He had recently left a staff meeting early after a news clip playing nearby and the sight of a uniformed officer in the corridor brought on such a vivid reliving that he had to lock himself in his office until it passed. What frightened Rafael most was not only the intensity of the memories, but the possibility that he would continue disappearing from his own life—cut off from colleagues, from culture, from ordinary freedom—while the men and institutions he believed had destroyed so much remained untouched. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget, but to stop living as though the cell door were still open somewhere just behind him.

violation_explanations: The vignette includes triggers and negative appraisals, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers lead to or intensify negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly show Rafael’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within a paragraph.
The vignette includes both negative appraisals and triggers, but it does not explicitly convey that his negative appraisals make triggers more likely to be noticed or experienced as triggers.
Although memories and negative appraisals both appear, the vignette does not explicitly state in the same paragraph that the trauma memory leads to or strengthens negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly convey that the trauma memory itself causes increased scanning for or sensitivity to triggers within a paragraph.

The vignette shows maladaptive strategies increasing alertness to danger signals and triggers, but it does not explicitly state that these strategies also lead to stronger negative appraisals or beliefs.
